paras: Dana Reyes has spent twenty-two years reading other people’s numbers, and she still describes the job the way she described it on her first week: most of it is boring, and the boring part is the work. She is a forensic accountant in Chicago. Companies call her when something does not close and nobody can say why. She has never once been called because somebody stole a large amount of money in one afternoon. That is not, she says, how any of it happens.

The turning point in her career came in 2009, and it came from something she was not looking for. She was checking a supplier list for a manufacturing client when she came across a parking receipt for eleven dollars, submitted twice in the same week. She corrected it and moved on. Three days later she saw it again. By the end of the month she had forty of them, and what she had was no longer a mistake. It was a pattern.

“A hunch is not evidence, and I have never pretended otherwise,” she says. “But a hunch tells you where to spend the next two weeks.” She looked into the expense system and ruled out a software error in the first four days. Then came the part she calls painstaking, and she means it as a compliment to the work rather than a complaint: eleven weeks of reading line items, one at a time, until the small thing pointed at a much larger one. She pieced the whole picture together from receipts, calendar entries and a single email that had been forwarded to the wrong person.

Her report held up. That word matters more to her than any other in the profession, because a report that does not hold up in front of a hostile lawyer is worse than no report at all. Since 2009 she has testified in nineteen cases, and she has never had a finding overturned. When people ask her how, she gives an answer that sounds like modesty and is not: she has simply never written a sentence she could not point at a document for.

The lesson she gives to people starting out has nothing to do with fraud. It is about size. Everybody, she says, is waiting for the enormous discrepancy, the one that announces itself. In twenty-two years she has never seen one arrive alone. There has always been a small one first, months earlier, sitting in a file that somebody looked at and decided was not worth the afternoon.

To show that the large problem is always announced by a small one that somebody decided to ignore.

listenings.text: People always ask me what a discrepancy looks like, and I think they are hoping for a story about a suitcase of cash. In twenty-two years I have never had that case. What it looks like is small, and it repeats. My favorite example is still the parking receipts, and I have told it so many times that my own team groans. Eleven dollars. Claimed twice a week, for two years. Nobody questioned it because eleven dollars is beneath the threshold where anybody looks, and that is exactly why it was eleven dollars. When we finally pulled the thread, the parking was not the problem. It was the smallest visible edge of something that had been running for four years in a different department entirely. And here is the part I want you to take away, because it has held true in every single review I have done since. I have never once seen a large discrepancy that did not have a small one in front of it, months earlier, sitting in a file that somebody opened and closed again.

In nineteen thirty-eight a physicist noticed something about the book of logarithm tables in his university library. The first pages were filthy and falling apart, and the last pages looked almost new. People had been looking up numbers that begin with one far more often than numbers that begin with nine, and there was no obvious reason why they should. It turned out there was a reason, and it holds across river lengths, street addresses, populations and the line items of a corporate expense report. In real data, roughly thirty percent of numbers begin with the digit one, and only about five percent begin with nine. Now consider what happens when a person sits down and invents a column of numbers. They spread the first digits out evenly, because even feels random to us, and evenly distributed is the one thing real data almost never is. Auditors have been using this since the nineteen nineties. It will not tell you who did it, and it will not tell you why. It only tells you that the shape is wrong, and that somebody should spend a week finding out what made it that shape.
